summary: This is a humorous RFC. It notes that TLS 1.3 key derivation uses a string of zero bytes as input when no pre-shared key is in use, and it jokingly proposes replacing those zeros with a hash of the audio of 2 Live Crew's "Banned in the U.S.A.". It is Informational and not something to deploy.

eli5.summary: Normally a secret lock starts with a blank code. This joke says to start it with a hash of a particular song instead.

questions: why is tls zero bytes a problem
subtitle: Replacing TLS 1.3's zero-byte key derivation input with a song hash.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.3 begins its key derivation by feeding zero bytes into the key schedule when no pre-shared key is in use, which is cryptographically fine but aesthetically troubling.
tldr.mechanism: This April Fools' document humorously proposes replacing those zeros with the SHA-256 digest of the uncompressed raw PCM audio of 2 Live Crew's 1990 album 'Banned in the U.S.A.', chosen because it survived institutional suppression and now represents the triumph of free speech in cryptography.
tldr.outcome: The joke illustrates the tension between cryptographic correctness and designer satisfaction, while celebrating both a censored work and the open internet through absurdist protocol design.

facts.label: Audio requirement
facts.value: Raw PCM, 1990 pressing, Track 1, lossless codec only

today: This is an April Fools' joke document published on April 1, 2026. It should not be deployed. The work it celebrates, 2 Live Crew's 'Banned in the U.S.A.', remains a real and important victory for free speech in music and media.

sections.title: The Zero-Byte Problem
sections.content: TLS 1.3 removes nearly all null cryptography, but one zero remains: in the PSK-free case, the key derivation function HKDF-Extract begins with a string of zero bytes as the input keying material (IKM). This April Fools' document proposes replacing those zeros with MAC (Mandatory Audio Component), defined as the SHA-256 digest of the raw PCM audio of 2 Live Crew's 'Banned in the U.S.A.' from their 1990 album, released on Luke Records.
sections.eli5: TLS 1.3 is a secret-making protocol that starts with nothing (zeros). This joke says to start with a hash of a famous song instead.

sections.title: Why This Song Matters
sections.content: The song 'Banned in the U.S.A.' was released in response to a 1990 federal court ruling that found 2 Live Crew's earlier album obscene. The Broward County Sheriff's Office arrested members of the group for performing in public. The conviction was overturned on appeal in 1992; the album was not obscene and free speech prevailed. The authors chose this work because it survived its own institutional suppression. By placing it at the root of the TLS key hierarchy, BUSA-TLS makes every byte of key derivation downstream from a work that defied censorship.
sections.eli5: This song was once banned and people were arrested for performing it. But the court said they were wrong, and free speech won. The joke is about putting that victory into a security protocol.

sections.title: The Technical Mechanism
sections.content: BUSA-TLS modifies RFC 8446's key schedule: instead of Early Secret = HKDF-Extract(salt=0, IKM=0), it uses Early Secret = HKDF-Extract(salt=0, IKM=MAC), where MAC is the SHA-256 hash of the canonical raw PCM audio (the 1990 pressing, track 1, lossless format only—no lossy compression). Both peers must use the same audio file or the connection fails at the Finished message verification. The document specifies two new TLS alert codes: one_very_important_thought (a warning) and banned_alert (fatal, for peers that lack the audio).
sections.eli5: Both sides of the connection must have the same song and compute its hash the same way. If one side does not have the song, the connection fails. It is intentional.

sections.title: Implementation Notes
sections.content: Implementations should cache the MAC (the song's hash) at startup because it does not change. The Mandatory Audio Component must be present on the host system at TLS handshake time; implementations must not fall back to zero-byte IKM if the audio is unavailable. The document notes that CI/CD environments that cannot lawfully obtain the album are the operator's problem, not the specification's. Modules validated under FIPS 140-3 would be 'a remarkable achievement' the authors would endorse enthusiastically, though validation is not planned.
sections.eli5: The implementation should remember the song's hash so it does not have to recompute it every time. If the song is missing, fail with an error message telling the operator to buy the album.
